records.title: King Arthur and the Lady of the Lake
records.summary: Following the shattering of his royal sword in single combat against King Pellinore, young King Arthur is guided by the enchanter Merlin to a mysterious, enchanted mountain tarn. From the mirrored waters of the lake, an ethereal arm clad in pure white samite rises to present the miraculous sword Excalibur and its magical scabbard, which prevents the bearer from losing blood. The Lady of the Lake (Nimue or Viviane) bestows the weapon upon Arthur with the solemn condition that when his mortal reign concludes, the blade must be returned to the water, fulfilling the destiny of Camelot.
alternate_names: Arthur Pendragon and the Lady of the Lake
records.historical_period: Medieval Matter of Britain (compiled 1485 in Le Morte d'Arthur by Sir Thomas Malory)
records.region_or_community: Cornwall, Somerset, and Welsh border marches

records.title: Robin Hood and the Sheriff of Nottingham
records.summary: Dwelling beneath the ancient boughs of the Major Oak in Sherwood Forest, outlaw nobleman Robin of Locksley commands a band of Merry Men—including Little John, Friar Tuck, and Will Scarlet—pledged to rob wealthy, corrupt Norman abbots and bailiffs to aid impoverished Saxon commoners. When the tyrannical Sheriff of Nottingham hosts a grand golden arrow archery tournament to lure Robin into an ambush, the outlaw enters disguised as a ragged tattered beggar. Splitting his rival's willow wand at the target's bullseye, Robin claims the golden arrow and escapes through Nottingham's gates with his men, mocking the sheriff.
alternate_names: The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood
records.historical_period: High Medieval Era (c. 13th–14th Century ballads, printed c. 1510 in A Gest of Robyn Hode)

records.title: Jack and the Beanstalk
records.summary: A poor country boy named Jack trades his widowed mother's solitary milking cow Milky-White for a handful of magical speckled beans. Furious at his foolishness, his mother flings the beans out the window into the cabbage patch. By morning, a colossal beanstalk has sprouted into the clouds. Climbing into the heavens, Jack discovers the sky castle of a fearsome man-eating giant who roars: 'Fee-fi-fo-fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman!' Using courage and stealth, Jack retrieves his family's stolen treasures: a bag of gold coins, a hen that lays golden eggs, and a singing golden harp, before chopping down the stalk as the giant pursues him.
alternate_names: The Story of Jack and the Bean-Stalk
records.historical_period: 18th Century English oral tradition (published 1807 by Benjamin Tabart, collected 1890 by Jacobs)

records.title: Lady Godiva of Coventry
records.summary: In 11th-century Coventry, Anglo-Saxon noblewoman Lady Godiva was moved to deep pity by the crushing, extortionate taxation imposed upon the townspeople by her harsh husband, Leofric, Earl of Mercia. Weary of her relentless petitions, Leofric sneeringly agreed to repeal the taxes on one impossible condition: Godiva must ride completely naked on horseback through the town market at high noon. Clothed only in her long, cascading golden hair, Godiva rode through the streets after issuing an edict that citizens keep shutters barred. Only a tailor named Tom bored a peep-hole in his wooden shutter, instantly struck blind for his insolence.
records.historical_period: Late Anglo-Saxon Era (c. 1040s historical figures, chronicled 13th Century by Roger of Wendover)

records.title: The Green Children of Woolpit
records.summary: During the 12th-century reign of King Stephen, harvesters in the Suffolk village of Woolpit discovered two young children—a boy and a girl—emerging from wolf-trapping pits in the earth. The children spoke an unintelligible language, wore clothing made of unfamiliar woven material, and had skin of a distinct greenish tint. Refusing all normal food, they wept until fed fresh green bean stalks. After being baptized, they lost their green hue. The surviving girl learned English and explained that they originated from 'Saint Martin's Land,' a sunless subterranean twilight country where all inhabitants are green, from which they wandered into the upper world following the chiming of distant church bells.
records.historical_period: Medieval Anglo-Norman Era (recorded c. 1189 by Ralph of Coggeshall and William of Newburgh)

records.title: Herne the Hunter of Windsor Great Park
records.summary: A legendary spectral huntsman of Berkshire folklore, Herne was a master forester to King Richard II who saved the monarch from a charging stag at the cost of mortal injury. Healed by a woodland sorcerer who bound the stag's antlers to his head, Herne incurred the malicious envy of fellow huntsmen, who framed him for royal poaching. Shamed, Herne hanged himself from an ancient oak in Windsor Great Park. For centuries, on stormy winter nights, his horned phantom leads a ghostly Wild Hunt across the royal forest astride a black steed, accompanied by howling hounds, rattling chains, and blasting hunting horns, withering vegetation where he rides.
records.historical_period: Late 14th Century setting (commemorated in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor, 1602)
records.region_or_community: Windsor Great Park and Berkshire countryside

records.title: The Lambton Worm of County Durham
records.summary: On a Sunday morning while skipping church, rebellious young heir John Lambton fished a repulsive, worm-like creature from the River Wear and discarded it into a nearby well. While Lambton fought in the Crusades, the worm grew into a colossal, venomous serpent with nine gill slits that terrorized County Durham, coiling nine times around Penshaw Hill and demanding the milk of nine cows daily. Returning a repentant knight, Lambton sought counsel from a wise witch, who advised him to forge armor studded with spearheads and fight the beast standing in the River Wear so the current would wash away severed chunks before they could rejoin.
records.historical_period: Medieval setting (c. 14th Century, celebrated in the 1867 folk song by C. M. Leumane)
records.region_or_community: County Durham and Wearside, North East England

records.title: Black Shuck: The Ghost Dog of East Anglia
records.summary: A terrifying spectral black hound the size of a calf with saucer-shaped flaming eyes, Black Shuck has prowled the marshes, graveyards, and coastlines of Norfolk and Suffolk for centuries. His most notorious historical manifestation occurred during a violent thunderstorm on Sunday, August 4, 1577, when the demon dog burst through the doors of Saint Mary's Church in Bungay, killing two kneeling parishioners and scorching the steeple before appearing simultaneously at Holy Trinity Church in Blythburgh, where he killed two more and left permanent claw scorch marks seared into the church's heavy oak north door.
records.historical_period: Tudor Era (August 4, 1577 documented storm) to Present
records.region_or_community: Norfolk and Suffolk coastal fens and marshes, East Anglia

records.title: Dick Whittington and His Cat
records.summary: An impoverished orphan from Gloucestershire named Dick Whittington walked to London hoping its streets were paved with gold. Finding only destitution, he was taken in as a scullery boy by a benevolent merchant, Mr. Fitzwarren. Dick bought a cat for a penny to catch the mice in his garret room. When the merchant asked his household to send ventures on a trading ship to the Barbary Coast, Dick offered his cat. Discouraged by the cook's cruelty, Dick packed his bundle to flee London, but pausing on Highgate Hill, he heard the chimes of Bow Bells calling: 'Turn again, Whittington, thrice Lord Mayor of London!' Returning, he learned the King of Barbary had bought his cat for an enormous fortune of jewels to rid his palace of rats.
alternate_names: The Lord Mayor and His Cat
records.historical_period: Late Medieval setting (Richard Whittington historical Mayor d. 1423, folklore printed 1605)

records.title: The Loch Ness Monster: Nessie and Saint Columba
records.summary: The earliest documented account of a water monster inhabiting Scotland's Loch Ness dates to 565 CE in Adomnán's Life of Saint Columba. While visiting the Pictish kingdom, the Irish saint encountered locals burying a man savaged by a water beast in the River Ness. Columba ordered a follower to swim across to retrieve a boat; when the monster lunged from the depths with open jaws, Columba made the sign of the cross and commanded: 'Go no further! Touch not the man! Go back with all speed!' The creature fled in terror as if pulled by ropes, initiating fifteen centuries of Scottish highland folklore culminating in modern cryptozoological sightings of 'Nessie.'
alternate_names: The Water Monster of the River Ness
records.historical_period: Early Medieval Era (565 CE recorded in 7th Century Vita Columbae by Adomnán)
